drawer.shortcutHint: Press ? to open help (when not typing in a field).

default.title: Help
default.summary: Contextual help for this screen has not been written yet.
default.body:
Use the sidebar to reach Dashboard, Integrations, Enrollments, and the other areas of the console. Your role — Global Admin or Tenant Admin — controls which items appear.

Press ? anytime to reopen this panel.

login.title: Signing in
login.summary: EZKey Admin uses passwordless approval on your enrolled device.
login.body:
Enter your admin username and submit. Approve the request in the EZKey mobile app when prompted. If you enabled “challenge code”, a two-digit code may appear here and on the device — they must match.

Sessions use a bearer token stored for this browser tab only.

Activation and recovery screens may show enrollment QR and binding challenge on screen (integrated delivery): Ezkey works without email or SMS adapters. You may still split those materials across your own channels for stronger assurance. Optional SMTP-assisted delivery can be configured later when the email channel is available.

dashboard.title: Dashboard
dashboard.summary: High-level counts and recent activity for your instance.
dashboard.body:
Cards summarize integrations, enrollments, and recent audit events. Auth Attempts (24h) lists every outcome in the rolling window; the badges sum to the headline total. Auth health (24h) uses completed attempts only for the percentage.

Timestamps use your selected language for formatting.
dashboard.authHealth: Auth health (24h): the headline is the success rate among completed attempts only (accepted, rejected, invalid, expired). Pending or in-flight attempts are excluded from that percentage. The Auth Attempts (24h) card next to it shows the full volume breakdown (in progress, accepted, rejected, invalid, expired) for the same window.
dashboard.globalContext: As a Global Admin, you see instance-wide metrics and can open tenant-scoped lists from here.
dashboard.tenantContext: As a Tenant (or Integration) Admin, counts are limited to your tenant and integrations you manage.
dashboard.demoExtra: Demo mode adds sample presets on some create forms and a badge in the header. It is removed from production builds.

tenants.title: Tenants
tenants.summary: Organizational units that own integrations, enrollments, and their own admin accounts.
tenants.body:
Each tenant groups a set of integrations, the users enrolled across them, and any Tenant Admins scoped to it. A tenant is either active or inactive — there is no delete: deactivation is the operationally complete answer for every offboarding and crisis scenario.

Deactivating a tenant immediately blocks all authentication for every integration and enrollment under it. No persistent change is made to any child record — they simply become non-operational until the tenant is reactivated. Reactivating restores full access instantly, with nothing left to reconcile. This makes tenant deactivation the fastest, safest tool for an emergency lockdown during a security incident.

This screen, like the Tenants list, appears only in the Global Admin navigation. Tenant Admins manage their own tenant's integrations, enrollments, and API keys from those dedicated screens instead.

tenant-detail.title: Tenant detail
tenant-detail.summary: One tenant's configuration, administrators, and lifecycle controls.
tenant-detail.body:
Review contact information, linked administrators, and lifecycle status. The Danger Zone shows activate/deactivate controls for non-system tenants — there is no delete for tenants; deactivation is the operationally complete answer to temporary suspension and offboarding alike.

Deactivating blocks all authentication downstream (integrations, enrollments) at runtime. The action is reversible at any time and leaves no lasting change on child records, so reactivating restores exactly the pre-incident state. Use it for temporary suspension or a security response.

The System Tenant is a protected root entity used for admin MFA; it cannot be deactivated, because doing so would take down the entire instance.

This screen, like the Tenants list, appears only in the Global Admin navigation.

integrations.title: Integrations
integrations.summary: Applications protected by EZKey MFA for a tenant.
integrations.body:
Each integration has a stable code, display name, and optional description. Its lifecycle has exactly two states — Active and Retired — with no intermediate “inactive” state: an application is either in service or being decommissioned. If you need to temporarily block access instead, deactivate the affected enrollments or revoke specific API keys — that is more precise and leaves a clearer audit trail.

Retiring an integration is permanent and requires a reason. It blocks new enrollments and blocks authentication through the eligibility chain, but existing enrollments and API keys keep their own state — nothing is revoked or deleted by retirement itself. Delete is only available once the integration is Retired and zero enrollments remain; it also requires a reason and should stay exceptional, reserved for housekeeping after every credential has already been dealt with individually.

An integration is “operational” when it is Active and its parent tenant is also active. If a tenant is deactivated, all its integrations show a warning even though their own status is Active — authentication is blocked until the tenant is reactivated.

Use search and filters to find integrations in large lists.
integrations.globalScope: As a Global Admin, you can view integrations across every tenant. New integrations you create land in the System Tenant — creating on behalf of a specific tenant is a Tenant Admin action, not something a Global Admin does for them.
integrations.tenantScope: As a Tenant Admin, you see and create integrations within your own tenant only; every integration you create is assigned to your tenant automatically.
integrations.demoExtra: With demo mode on, "Fill demo" presets appear in the create dialog to speed up local testing.

integration-detail.title: Integration detail
integration-detail.summary: One integration's configuration and related objects.
integration-detail.body:
Review identifiers, lifecycle status, and related resources. An integration is “operational” when it is Active and its parent tenant is active — only operational integrations can process authentications.

Retiring an integration is permanent and requires a reason. It blocks new enrollments and blocks authentication through the eligibility chain — but existing enrollments and API keys keep their own state and are not revoked or deleted by the retirement itself; they simply become non-operational, the same way they would under an inactive tenant.

Delete is only available once the integration is Retired and zero enrollments remain; it also requires a reason and should stay exceptional — reserved for cleanup after every credential has already been resolved individually (revoked, deleted, or migrated), not as a shortcut around retirement.

From here you can manage enrollments, create API keys (while Active), and trigger bulk enrollment operations in the danger zone.

enrollments.title: Enrollments
enrollments.summary: User-device bindings that enable MFA authentication for an integration.
enrollments.body:
Each enrollment links one user's device to an integration and moves through Created → Bound → Verified. Only Verified and active enrollments can process authentication attempts.

Deactivate when you are not sure yet — a lost-device report, a security alert, an investigation still in progress. It blocks authentication within seconds and is fully reversible: reactivating restores access immediately with the same credential, no re-enrollment needed. Revoke when you are sure — a confirmed compromise, a user who has left. Revocation is permanent and requires a reason; the device key is invalidated and the user needs a brand-new enrollment.

An enrollment is “operational” when it is Verified, active, and its full parent chain (integration and tenant) is also active. If an integration is retired or a tenant is deactivated, all their enrollments show an operational warning even though their own status is still Verified. A warning triangle in the status column flags this parent-chain degradation.

Integrated delivery: create and detail screens can show the enrollment QR and binding challenge directly in the Admin UI so the instance works without email or SMS. Splitting those materials across your own channels (screenshot, SMS, chat) remains a valid operator practice; optional SMTP-assisted delivery can be configured later once the email channel is available.
enrollments.globalScope: As a Global Admin, this list spans every tenant; a tenant column shows which organization each enrollment belongs to.
enrollments.tenantScope: As a Tenant Admin, you see and manage only the enrollments that belong to your own tenant.

enrollment-detail.title: Enrollment detail
enrollment-detail.summary: One user-device binding, its lifecycle actions, and associated cryptographic material.
enrollment-detail.body:
This screen shows the enrollment status, contact information, key tier, and proof token. Test Authentication triggers a live MFA request to the enrolled device — the button is disabled when the enrollment is not operational.

Deactivating suspends authentication without any permanent change; reactivating restores it immediately with the same credential. Revoking is permanent and requires a reason — the device key is invalidated and the user needs a brand-new enrollment. Delete removes the record entirely and also requires a reason, but only when there is zero authentication history and the enrollment is not linked as any admin's MFA credential.

Revoke is preferred over delete for security-motivated actions because it preserves a complete audit trail. Delete is reserved for cleaning up test data or genuine mistakes that were never actually used.

When bind material is still available, integrated delivery shows the proof token, QR, and binding challenge here without requiring email or SMS adapters. You may split those materials across your own channels for stronger assurance.

auth-attempts.title: Auth attempts
auth-attempts.summary: A read-only trail of individual MFA decision events tied to enrollments.
auth-attempts.body:
Auth attempts are created and resolved automatically by the eligibility chain — this is not an entity you create, edit, or manage directly. An attempt can only be created when its enrollment is Verified and active, its integration is Active, and its tenant is active.

Status moves from Pending (waiting for the device) through Read (the device has fetched it) to one final outcome: Accepted, Rejected, Expired (no response in time), or Invalid (a signature or challenge check failed). Once an attempt reaches a final status it never changes again.

The challenge column, when present, is the optional two-digit code the user compares between this screen and their device — a visual cross-check, not a secret.

Use this screen to investigate a specific login or authentication episode, or open the linked audit trail for one attempt for the full surrounding context. See the Audit Logs help for how passwordless sign-in events relate to session outcomes.

api-keys.title: API Keys
api-keys.summary: Secret keys that authenticate Integration API requests for a specific integration.
api-keys.body:
API keys are scoped to one integration. Their lifecycle is intentionally asymmetric compared to every other entity: a key can be created and revoked, but never deactivated, reactivated, or deleted. There is no “temporarily suspend a key” state — if you need to pause access, revoke it and issue a new one; that removes any ambiguity about whether an old key might still work somewhere.

Revoking is permanent and requires a reason. Revoked keys are kept permanently for audit traceability — deleting one would leave a gap in the trail for every API call it ever authenticated. Keys can also expire automatically based on their configured time-to-live; expiration needs no operator action or reason.

An API key is “operational” when it is Active, not expired, and its parent integration and tenant are both active. A blocked-by-parent warning means the key itself is valid but authentication would fail at runtime because of its parent chain.

Secret values are shown only once, at creation — copy them immediately. Use IP whitelists to restrict where a key can be used; a maximum of 5 active keys is enforced per integration to keep rotation manageable.

api-key-detail.title: API Key detail
api-key-detail.summary: One API key, its configuration, and revocation controls.
api-key-detail.body:
This screen shows the key identifiers, IP whitelist, status, and usage history. You can edit the description and IP whitelist for active keys.

Revoking an API key is permanent and irreversible — the key can no longer authenticate Integration API requests. A reason is required for audit. Plan key rotation in advance (create the replacement first) to avoid a service interruption.

admins.title: Administrators
admins.summary: Global and Tenant administrators who operate Ezkey through the Admin UI.
admins.body:
Global Admins manage instance-wide concerns — encryption keys, all tenants, platform alerts. Tenant Admins are scoped to one tenant and manage its integrations, enrollments, and API keys. Every admin authenticates with MFA on their own enrolled device, exactly like an end user.

An admin has three lifecycle states: Pending Activation (identity created, first-time setup not completed), Active (normal operation), and Deactivated (suspended by an operator). Deactivating suspends login without deleting the account or touching the admin's MFA enrollment — revoking that enrollment is a separate action, done from the enrollment's own detail screen. Two safety guards always apply: an admin cannot deactivate themselves, and Ezkey never lets the last active Global Admin be deactivated. In the current console, deactivating or reactivating any admin is a Global Admin action, regardless of which tenant the admin belongs to.

Activation and recovery look similar on screen but are different concepts: activation establishes an admin's first-ever enrollment; recovery re-establishes access for an admin who already had one (for example after losing a device). Onboarding and recovery dialogs use integrated delivery — proof token, QR, and binding challenge appear directly in the Admin UI without email or SMS adapters; splitting those materials across your own channels remains a valid practice, and optional SMTP-assisted delivery can be configured later once the email channel is available.
admins.recoveryCodes: Recovery codes are a separate, admin-only safety net for regaining access when the enrolled device is unavailable — regular end-user enrollments do not have them. They exist independently of the admin's MFA enrollment: revoking the enrollment does not invalidate recovery codes, and regenerating codes does not touch the enrollment. “Issue initial” appears for an admin who has logged in at least once but never had a set; “Regenerate” replaces an existing set entirely — every unused code from the previous set stops working the moment the new set is issued.

encryption-keys.title: Encryption keys
encryption-keys.summary: Instance-wide AES keys for data at rest and re-encryption batches.
encryption-keys.body:
The PRIMARY key encrypts new data. Older keys stay ENABLED until every row that used them is migrated to a newer key.

A re-encryption batch is one job per table column and old key: it moves ciphertext to the current PRIMARY. “Create batches” only queues work; “Trigger full re-encryption” creates and processes batches in one step; “Resume” retries a pending or failed batch. Per-key “Re-encrypt” targets one old key.

The scheduled job also creates and processes batches—new rows created late in a run may wait for the next run unless you trigger or resume manually.
encryption-keys.globalOps: As a Global Admin you manage keys for the whole instance. Tenant admins do not use this screen.
encryption-keys.developerContext: Ciphertext uses the ENC:keyId:… prefix so the system can count rows per key. Discoverable targets are defined in code (Reencryptable entities). For full endpoint semantics and diagrams, see docs/REENCRYPTION_OPERATIONS.md in the repository.

audit-logs.title: Audit logs
audit-logs.summary: A read-only trail of security-relevant actions and outcomes across Ezkey. Use it to see who did what, whether the step succeeded, and to support investigations.
audit-logs.body:
Each row is an immutable record: Ezkey does not rewrite history after the fact. Events come from the Admin API and related services (the API column shows the source).

Use filters—event type, status, API name, and date range—to narrow the list. Open a row for identifiers (admin, integration, enrollment, auth attempt) when present, and for extra detail or error text.

Your role determines which events you can see: Global Admins have broader visibility; Tenant Admins see activity tied to their tenant where policies allow.
audit-logs.eventTypeVsStatus:
Two columns work together:

• Event type — the category of operation (for example admin login, enrollment created, API key revoked). It answers “what kind of event is this?”

• Status — how that operation finished for the audited step. Success means the step completed as intended. Failure means an expected outcome stopped the flow (validation, policy, or a normal terminal result such as an expired or rejected MFA attempt). Error means something unexpected went wrong while processing the request and may warrant investigation.

For automation and exports: Failure is the usual status for “expected” denials and terminal MFA outcomes; Error points to unexpected processing failures—correlate with server logs if needed. The event action value is the stable field for filters and SIEM rules.
audit-logs.statusLegend:
Success — the audited step completed successfully.
Failure — the step did not complete in the expected success path; details often appear in the row or error message.
Error — unexpected failure; treat as worth reviewing in logs or support.
audit-logs.mfaAndLogin: Passwordless admin sign-in can take two steps. The first step may only create an MFA request on your enrolled device: a Success status there means the request was accepted by the server, not that you already hold a session. A separate entry shows when a session is issued or when the attempt ended without a session (for example expired, rejected, or timed out), once those outcomes are recorded for the wait step.
audit-logs.integrityNote: Chain checkpoints, seal archive, and declare gap are advanced integrity operations. Use the inline help (?) next to each section on this page for how and when to use them.

alerts.title: Alerts
alerts.summary: Platform-raised signals about audit-chain health and integrity, visible to Global Admins.
alerts.body:
Alerts are raised automatically by platform services — for example when a scheduled audit-chain check detects an undeclared gap, or when heartbeat supervision goes stale. Each alert has a severity (Critical, Warning, Info) and a status: Open (needs attention) or Resolved (the underlying condition was addressed).

Open alerts are deduplicated: while the same condition persists, Ezkey updates the existing open alert's last-seen time and occurrence count instead of creating a duplicate. Most alert types resolve themselves automatically once the underlying condition clears — for example, declaring a gap resolves the matching gap alert. An audit integrity rupture is the one type that needs a deliberate operator action: open the alert and use Reconcile to record a signed conciliation checkpoint together with a justification.

This is a Global Admin surface — integrity monitoring and remediation are platform-level concerns; Tenant Admins do not see it.

alert-detail.title: Alert detail
alert-detail.summary: One alert's details, payload, and — for integrity ruptures — the reconciliation action.
alert-detail.body:
Most alerts are informational once you open them: the Details and Resolution cards show when the alert was raised, how many times the same condition recurred, and — once resolved — when, and why. Gap and heartbeat alerts typically resolve on their own once you declare the gap or supervision recovers; there is nothing to click here for those.

Audit integrity rupture alerts are the exception. While the alert is Open, a Reconcile action re-verifies the affected window live, asks you to acknowledge any entry violations that still need it, and records a signed conciliation checkpoint together with a classification and justification. This is the only way an integrity rupture alert moves to Resolved, and it is irreversible for that alert.

Use the “Open in audit logs” / “Investigate in Audit Logs” links on the payload to jump straight to the affected window.
